stories.headline: S&P 500 CLIMBS TO 7,575 AS NVIDIA AND META LEAD A TECH SURGE, SK HYNIX POPS 13% IN $26.5B DEBUT
stories.body: The S&P 500 gained 0.42% to close at 7,575.39 and the Nasdaq-100 rose roughly 0.85%, powered by Nvidia (+4.0%) and Meta (+6.0% after a Bank of America note flagged lower-than-expected internal AI computing costs), while South Korean memory-chip maker SK Hynix soared 13% in its $26.5 billion U.S. listing debut.
stories.explain: Meta's rally on a cost memo rather than a revenue beat matters because AI capex bulls and bears are really debating the same number: how much compute a dollar of spending buys, and cheaper-than-expected inference costs directly raise the operating margin the market prices into every AI-linked stock, not just Meta's. SK Hynix's 13% pop is the same trade from the supply side — it is one of two dominant producers of the high-bandwidth memory chips that feed Nvidia's AI accelerators, so a hot U.S. listing signals investors betting memory demand from AI clusters stays structurally elevated rather than fading. Today's Deep Dive turns to a different mechanism sitting one line below: how oil's slide is already working its way into Tuesday's CPI print.

stories.headline: OIL EXTENDS SLIDE AS TRUMP SAYS IRAN HAS REACHED OUT TO NEGOTIATE, DEFLATING THE WAR-RISK PREMIUM FURTHER
stories.body: WTI crude fell about 1.0% to roughly $71.90 and Brent slipped toward $75.50, extending Thursday's more-than-2% drop, after President Trump said Iran had reached out about restarting negotiations — even though Brent remains on pace for a roughly 4-5% gain on the week given how far the war-risk premium had spiked earlier.
stories.explain: This is the same repricing mechanism from Wednesday's Iran-strike spike running in reverse: traders aren't pricing that the conflict ended, they're pricing that the specific tail scenario — a closed Strait of Hormuz or seized tankers — is now less likely given an active diplomatic channel, so the premium bleeds out even before any deal is signed. The move is a reminder that oil's risk premium tracks the probability of disruption, which can swing on a single reported phone call, while the fundamental supply-demand price underneath moves far more slowly.

stories.headline: 10-YEAR YIELD SLIPS TO 4.55% AS OIL'S RETREAT EASES INFLATION FEARS AHEAD OF TUESDAY'S CPI
stories.body: The 10-year Treasury yield eased about 3 basis points to 4.55% while the 2-year held flat at 4.19%, narrowing the 10s2s spread to roughly 36 basis points, as crude's second straight day of declines took some pressure off inflation expectations heading into Tuesday's June CPI report and the July 28-29 FOMC meeting.
stories.explain: The 10-year yield embeds a term premium that reacts to input-cost inflation risk, so two days of falling oil prices mechanically lowers the market's expected path of headline CPI and, with it, the compensation investors demand for holding longer-dated debt. The 2-year holding flat at 4.19% shows the Fed's near-term policy path is unchanged by this — futures still price close to zero odds of a 2026 cut — meaning today's move is entirely a long-end story about the inflation outlook, not a shift in what the Fed does at its next meeting.

stories.headline: GOLD SLIPS 0.3% TO $4,111 AS RISK-ON RALLY AND FADING WAR-RISK PREMIUM SAP SAFE-HAVEN DEMAND
stories.body: Gold eased about 0.3% to roughly $4,111/oz even as the dollar index also softened to about 100.85 (-0.1%), an unusual case of gold and the dollar falling together as today's equity rally and Iran de-escalation signals reduced appetite for safe havens on both fronts at once.
stories.explain: Gold and the dollar are typically inversely correlated because a weaker dollar lowers the cost of gold for foreign buyers, so both falling together signals a genuine risk-on rotation is overriding that usual relationship — traders are selling safety broadly (gold) rather than rotating between two different safe assets. That gold gave back ground on the same day equities and oil both moved on de-escalation news suggests today's price action is about receding tail risk more than any specific rates or dollar catalyst.

stories.headline: ST. JOHN'S DONNIE FREEMAN OUT FOR SEASON AS OFFSEASON PORTAL CHAOS TOPS 2,700 TRANSFERS
stories.body: Red Storm forward Donnie Freeman will miss all of 2026-27 after rupturing his Achilles in a team workout and undergoing surgery, a major blow to a St. John's roster already reshaped by the transfer portal. More than 2,700 players have entered the portal since the season ended — the largest offseason player-movement wave on record — while five-star guard Marcus Spears Jr. reclassified to 2026 to join Texas.

stories.headline: VICTOR WEMBANYAMA TAKES LESS THAN MAX ON $252M SPURS EXTENSION TO BUILD AROUND HIM FASTER
stories.body: Wembanyama and San Antonio agreed to a five-year, $252 million rookie-scale extension — the 25% max tier instead of the 30% supermax that could have paid him $303 million — a deal that could save the Spurs roughly $50 million in cap space over five years to build a contender around him. Elsewhere, Cleveland locked up Donovan Mitchell on a four-year, $273 million extension and Memphis traded Ja Morant to Portland.

stories.headline: TERRION ARNOLD DRAWS INTEREST FROM FOUR TEAMS DESPITE FELONY CHARGES, STILL UNSIGNED
stories.body: The cornerback Detroit released June 29 after his arrest on eight felony charges tied to a February robbery and kidnapping in Tampa has now worked out for or drawn inquiries from the Texans, Colts, Jets and Seahawks, per his agent, who says there's a 'very good likelihood' Arnold signs somewhere within 45 days. He remains restricted to his Florida home except for work- or legal-related travel under his release conditions.

stories.headline: PAC-12 OFFICIALLY BACK AT FBS STATUS AS TEXAS STATE JOINS AS EIGHTH FOOTBALL MEMBER
stories.body: Texas State's move from the Sun Belt made the Pac-12 whole again as of July 1, clearing the NCAA's eight-team minimum for FBS status and completing the conference's rebuild after realignment gutted it in 2023-24. Elsewhere, ESPN's preseason FPI opened with Ohio State No. 1 and Oregon getting a boost after Dante Moore passed on the NFL draft to return at quarterback.

deepDive.title: How Falling Oil Actually Flows Through Into Tuesday's CPI Print
content: Oil closed out the week down for a second straight session, with WTI easing about 1.0% to roughly $71.90 as an Iran diplomatic opening deflated the war-risk premium, and that decline is a direct reason the 10-year Treasury yield slipped 3 basis points to 4.55% Friday. The connection isn't abstract: energy prices feed mechanically into the CPI report due Tuesday, the last inflation read before the Fed's July 28-29 meeting, and traders are already repricing rate expectations off a number that hasn't been published yet. Understanding exactly how oil gets from a barrel price into a CPI percentage — and where that channel runs dry — is the difference between reading Tuesday's release correctly and overreacting to a number that doesn't actually move the Fed.

The mechanism is narrower than most people assume. Energy makes up about 6.5-7% of the CPI basket, with motor fuel (mostly gasoline) accounting for roughly 3.5 points of that; the Bureau of Labor Statistics samples retail gas prices directly, so a drop in WTI shows up in headline CPI within two to three weeks as it works through refining margins and pump prices. But the Fed's preferred gauge is core CPI, which strips out food and energy entirely, precisely because oil is volatile enough to swing month to month for reasons that have nothing to do with underlying demand. Oil still touches core indirectly — through freight and airfare costs, and through the energy inputs baked into goods prices — but that pass-through is slower and much smaller than the direct headline effect.

The clearest illustration is 2015, when WTI collapsed from over $100 to under $30 a barrel and headline CPI went negative on a year-over-year basis for several months, even as core CPI held close to 2% the entire time. The Fed didn't treat the headline print as evidence of disinflation risk requiring a policy response; officials explicitly looked through it as an energy-specific, not demand-driven, move — a distinction that mattered enormously for how slowly liftoff proceeded that cycle. Base effects compound this: because CPI is measured year-over-year, a report can look tame or hot largely based on where oil sat twelve months earlier, independent of what happened this month. Tuesday's comparison point is last July's price level, not today's $71.90.

For Tuesday, the setup is straightforward: two days of falling oil should soften the headline MoM print relative to where it would've landed without the Iran de-escalation news, while core CPI — driven by shelter, services, and the pass-through of tariff costs into goods prices — is the number that actually informs the July 28-29 decision. If headline comes in soft purely on energy while core surprises hot, expect yields to reverse Friday's move quickly, since a benign gasoline number doesn't change the Fed's calculus. The 10s2s spread sitting at just 36 basis points already signals a market pricing very little cutting room this year; a hot core print is the one input that could actually widen that spread by pushing the long end higher on renewed inflation risk.
